162.title: If you will (Mark 1:40–45)
162.hook: a man with leprosy says if you are willing; Jesus, moved, touches him
162.howItsDone: Many Christians take this story as a call to reach people who are isolated, and Christian groups have long run hospitals and missions for people with leprosy and other stigmatized illnesses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: diakoneō, to serve, and prayer a great while before day. Your line was a great while before day.

A handshake, a hug, a hand on a shoulder: small touches nobody counts until they stop. For the man in today's story, they had stopped. He had a skin disease the Bible calls leprosy, and the law said he had to live outside the town, clothes torn, calling out a warning so nobody came near. Nobody touched him. Nobody was supposed to. Then one day, breaking every rule of distance, he walks straight up to Jesus and kneels.
screen: `NO HANDSHAKE, NO HUG.` → `OUTSIDE THE TOWN, CALLING A WARNING.` → `HE KNEELS IN FRONT OF JESUS.`

segments.voice: Leper is the old word for a person with leprosy. Some people now prefer to say a person with leprosy, because leper came to mean an outcast, and this man was one. In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of skin diseases, not only what doctors now call Hansen's disease. Leviticus says such a person "shall cry, Unclean, unclean," and "he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his habitation be." He asks, in the King James Bible: "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." He's sure Jesus can. His question is whether Jesus wants to. That's the question under a lot of human pain: not is it possible, but does anyone want to? Then Mark: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean." I will. I am willing. And before a word of healing, a touch, while the man is still unclean by the law's own terms. Under the purity laws, uncleanness could pass by touch. Mark tells it the other way round: Jesus touches, and the man is made clean. A few old manuscripts say not moved with compassion, but moved with anger. Anger at the disease, perhaps, or at his isolation. Scholars still debate which reading is original. Jesus tells the man to tell no one, and to show himself to the priest as the law required. The man tells everyone. Now Jesus can't openly enter a town; he stays out in the lonely places. The outsider comes in, and Jesus ends up outside.

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your own shoulder, or over your heart, and notice what a kind touch feels like. Then hold the face of someone who may not have been touched kindly in a while: an older neighbor, a friend living alone, someone grieving, someone everyone keeps at a distance. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well, and think of one appropriate, kind touch you could offer: a handshake, a hug, a hand on a shoulder.
Leper. A person with a skin disease who, by law, lived alone outside the town. Jesus touched him first.
Your line: I am willing. The touch came before the word. That's day one hundred sixty-two.

163.title: Through the roof (Mark 2:1–12)
163.hook: four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus
163.howItsDone: Many Christians pray for friends by name, and churches often keep prayer lists and send people to visit, cook for or drive those who are sick, a practice some connect with the four friends on the roof.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a man with leprosy knelt, and Jesus touched him. Your line was I am willing.

Capernaum again, and word is out that Jesus is home. The house fills. Then the doorway. Then the street outside. Up the lane come four men carrying a fifth on a mat. He can't walk. They've carried him all this way, and now there's a wall of backs between them and the one person they came for. The easy thing would be to stand at the edge of that crowd, sigh, and carry him home. Tomorrow, maybe. These four look up.
screen: `A HOUSE FULL TO THE DOOR.` → `FOUR MEN, ONE MAT.` → `THEY LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: A Galilean village roof was usually flat: wooden beams, branches laid across, and a thick layer of packed clay on top. So the four climb up and start digging; Mark's Greek word means digging out a hole. Picture it from inside. Jesus is teaching, and dirt starts falling on everyone's heads. A patch of light opens. Then a man on a mat comes down on ropes. In the King James Bible: "they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay." Then a small phrase: "When Jesus saw their faith." Their faith, not only the man on the mat's. Mark notices the four on the roof, sweating, clay under their nails. Their stubbornness counted. And Jesus's first words surprise everyone: "Son, thy sins be forgiven thee." Some teachers of the law think, who can forgive sins but God alone? Jesus answers with a question: which is easier to say, your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk? Then he tells the man to pick up his mat and go home, and he does, out through the crowd that wouldn't let him in. Christians read this in more than one way. Some hear a claim about who Jesus is, since he speaks the forgiveness the scribes say belongs to God alone. Others hear it about friendship: someone can be carried to healing by other people's faith. The crowd's verdict is the last line: "We never saw it on this fashion." Nobody had.

Ask what digging would look like: a second phone call when the first went unanswered, showing up with food instead of offering, driving them, asking again. If you pray, carry them before God the way the four carried that mat, one corner each; if you don't, hold them in mind and choose your one stubborn thing.

Your line: friends who dig through roofs. Four friends, one mat, one roof. See you tomorrow.

164.title: Levi's table (Mark 2:13–17)
164.hook: the healthy don't need a doctor; he came for sinners
164.carry: the doctor is for the sick
164.howItsDone: Many churches remember Levi's dinner in shared meals open to anyone, such as community suppers and food programs, and Christians often point to this passage when welcoming people who feel unwelcome elsewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four men dug through a clay roof to lower their paralytic friend to Jesus. Your line was friends who dig through roofs.

Some towns have one person everybody agrees is on the wrong side. Not a criminal, exactly. Just the one nobody wants at the barbecue. In Capernaum that man sat in a booth by the road, taking tolls. His name was Levi. Jesus walks past the booth and says: follow me. Just like that, Mark says, he got up and followed. Then the gossip starts. There's a dinner at Levi's house, full of his friends, the ones decent people crossed the street to avoid. And Jesus sits down with them.
screen: `A TOLL BOOTH BY THE ROAD.` → `FOLLOW ME.` → `A HOUSE FULL OF THE WRONG PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Tax collectors in Galilee gathered tolls and duties on goods moving along the roads, for Herod's government, which answered to Rome. They were widely suspected of taking extra for themselves, and neighbors could see them as working for the occupier. So when the King James Bible says Jesus sat with "publicans and sinners", publicans being the old word for tax collectors, it means people who were written off. And in that world, eating together wasn't small. A shared table said: we belong together. Some scribes of the Pharisees ask the disciples, why does he eat with these people? It's a fair question in their world. They cared deeply about holiness, and holiness has a lot to do with who you let close. Jesus overhears, and answers with a picture anyone can understand: "They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." A doctor who only visits healthy people isn't much of a doctor. Some Christians hear good news here for anyone who feels too far gone: the table is set for exactly those people. Others hear a gentle question for the ones who feel healthy: are you sure? One more detail. Matthew's gospel tells the same story and calls the tax collector Matthew. Christian tradition has long taken Levi and Matthew to be the same man, so the toll collector may be the one whose name is on a gospel.

165.title: New wine (Mark 2:18–22)
165.hook: you don't pour new wine into old skins
165.howItsDone: Most churches keep seasons of fasting, especially Lent before Easter, and many Christians connect them with Jesus's words that his followers would fast once the bridegroom was taken away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Levi's table, a tax collector's dinner, and Jesus sitting with the people nobody sat with. Your line was the doctor is for the sick.

Someone at work notices you're not doing it the way it's always been done. Not wrong, just different. And they ask, a little sharply, why? That's where today's story starts. The followers of John the Baptist fast. The Pharisees fast. Serious religious people go without food on set days, and everyone knows it. But Jesus's followers are eating. So people ask him straight out: why don't your disciples fast? He answers with a wedding, a patched coat, and a wineskin about to burst.

First the wedding. In the King James Bible: "Can the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them?" The children of the bridechamber are the wedding guests. Nobody fasts at a wedding. You eat, you dance, the party goes for days. While the groom is here, Jesus says, it's a feast. But he adds a shadow: the day will come when the groom is taken away, and then they'll fast. Christians hear that as his first hint at his death, and it's why most churches still keep fasts, in Lent and on other days. Then the coat. You don't sew a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old coat; the first wash, it shrinks and tears a worse hole. Then the wine. "No man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles." A bottle here is a skin, usually goat, not glass. New wine is still fermenting, still giving off gas, so it needs a fresh skin that can stretch. An old skin is dry and stiff; it splits, and you lose both. So what's the new wine? Christians usually say it's what Jesus himself brings, and that it needs room to move. How that applies is argued in every generation, from reformers to people who start a new kind of church in a coffee shop. And Luke, telling the same story, adds a line that keeps everyone humble: people who have drunk the old wine say the old is better. New wine isn't a verdict on the old. It's a question of what can hold it.

Don't throw it out; just pick one small change, a different time, a different word, a different route, and hold it lightly.
New wine. Wine still fermenting, too alive for an old stiff skin. It needs a vessel that can stretch.

166.title: Lord of the sabbath (Mark 2:23–28)
166.hook: the disciples pick grain on the sabbath, and Jesus defends them
166.howItsDone: Christians in many churches keep Sunday as a day of worship and rest in honor of the resurrection, while some churches, such as Seventh-day Adventists, keep the seventh day, Saturday, as the sabbath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a wedding, a patched coat and a wineskin. Your line was new wine, new skins.

A Saturday in Galilee. The grain is high on both sides of a footpath. Jesus and his friends are hungry, so as they walk, the disciples pull off a few heads of grain, rub them in their hands and eat. Anyone could; the law of Moses let a passerby pick by hand from a neighbor's field. The trouble is the day. It's the sabbath, the day of rest, and to some Pharisees watching, picking grain looks like harvesting, and harvesting is work. Why, they ask, are your disciples doing what isn't allowed?
screen: `A PATH THROUGH THE GRAIN.` → `HUNGRY HANDS.` → `BUT IT'S THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: First, how much the sabbath mattered, and still matters. It's one of the Ten Commandments: one day in seven, no work, for everyone, including servants, foreigners and animals. For Jews it was, and is, a gift and a sign of belonging to God, kept with real joy. So the Pharisees' question is serious, not petty; what counts as work is exactly what careful people argued about. Jesus answers first from scripture. Remember David, he says, when he and his men were hungry, and the priest gave them the holy bread from the house of God, bread only priests were meant to eat. Need came first. Then the line, in the King James Bible: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." And one more sentence, the one that gives today its title: "Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath." In the gospels, Son of Man is how Jesus often speaks of himself. So this isn't only a ruling about grain; Christian readers hear him claiming the right to say what the day of rest is for. A neighbor shares the first half. Jewish teachers also taught that saving a life outweighs the sabbath, and one early rabbinic teaching says something very close: the sabbath is given to you, not you to the sabbath. Many churches keep Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as their day of rest and worship. Some, like Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday. Either way the question stays the same: is my rest healing me?
screen: `ONE DAY IN SEVEN, FOR EVERYONE.` · `DAVID AND THE HOLY BREAD.` · `THE SABBATH WAS MADE FOR MAN.` · `LORD ALSO OF THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Ask your body what kind of tired it is: sleepy tired, needing a nap; people tired, needing quiet; screen tired, needing a window and some sky; worried tired, needing to put something down. Your line: made for people. Need came first. Day one hundred sixty-six is all yours.

167.title: The withered hand (Mark 3:1–6)
167.hook: he looks around in anger at hard hearts, and heals on the sabbath anyway
167.howItsDone: Many Christians read this passage as a call to do good without waiting for the convenient moment, and churches often hold healing services or pray for the sick with hands outstretched or laid on them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hungry friends in a grain field, and the sabbath defended as a gift. Your line was made for people.

A meeting where everyone is waiting to see which side someone will take: that's the mood in this synagogue, on a sabbath. Jesus walks in, and there's a man whose hand is withered, shrunken and useless. Mark says some people there are watching Jesus, not the man, to see whether he'll heal on the sabbath, so they'll have something against him. The man has become a test case. Jesus knows it. The whole room knows it. And Mark says what Jesus felt.
screen: `A ROOM THAT'S WATCHING.` → `A MAN WITH A WITHERED HAND.` → `A TEST CASE.`

segments.voice: Jesus doesn't do it quietly in a corner. He tells the man, stand up in the middle. Then he turns to the room, in the King James Bible: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?" It's a question with only one decent answer. "But they held their peace." Then comes the verse Mark keeps and the other gospels soften: "when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand." Anger and grief in the same breath. Hardness here is a word for skin gone thick and stiff, like a callus: a heart that can't feel anymore. The man stretches out his hand, and it's restored, whole as the other. Jesus doesn't touch him. He just asks him to do the one thing his hand couldn't: reach. And the ending is dark. Some Pharisees go out and start planning with supporters of King Herod how to destroy Jesus. Three chapters in, and already there's a plot. Readers take a few things from this. That doing good is never out of season. That Jesus's anger is real, and aimed at hard hearts, not at hurting people. And that sometimes the healing starts when someone asks you to stretch toward what you think you can't do.
screen: `STAND UP IN THE MIDDLE.` · `TO SAVE LIFE, OR TO KILL?` · `ANGER AND GRIEF AT HARD HEARTS.` · `STRETCH FORTH THINE HAND.`

If you pray, open your hand to God; then let it rest.
Hardness, the callused heart Jesus grieved over in the watching room, right before he told the man to stretch out his hand.
Your line: stretch out your hand. Doing good is never out of season. That's day one hundred sixty-seven.

168.title: Twelve names (Mark 3:7–19)
168.hook: he calls twelve to be with him and to be sent, including the one who'll betray him
168.howItsDone: Christians honor the twelve apostles, and many churches keep feast days for them through the year; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches describe their bishops as standing in succession from the apostles, while many Protestant churches speak of being apostolic by holding to the apostles' teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a man stood up in the middle of a watching room, and Jesus grieved their hardness. Your line was stretch out your hand. Twenty-four weeks now.

By now the crowds are enormous. Mark lists where they come from: Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, the desert country to the south, across the Jordan, even the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. So many that Jesus asks for a small boat to stand by, in case he's crushed on the shore. And right then, at the height of it, he walks away. He goes up into the hills and calls a handful of people by name. Not the biggest donors or the best speakers. Fishermen. A tax collector. A man who'll one day hand him over.
screen: `CROWDS FROM EVERYWHERE.` → `A BOAT STANDING BY.` → `UP INTO THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach." Two jobs, in that order. First, to be with him. Then, to be sent. The Greek for one who is sent is apostolos, where English gets apostle. So an apostle isn't first a manager or a speaker; in Mark, it's someone who has been with Jesus before being sent anywhere. Why twelve? Israel had twelve tribes, and some readers hear Jesus gathering a renewed people around him, one for each tribe. Then Mark reads out the names, like a roll call. Simon, whom he names Peter, which means rock. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom he nicknames "Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder." Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, another James, Thaddaeus, another Simon, called the Zealot or the Canaanite. And the last name comes with a note nobody would put in a founding document: "Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him." Mark tells you before you've grown attached. Jesus chose him anyway, and kept him close to the end. That closes a week in Mark: a man with leprosy, touched; four friends through a roof; Levi's table; new wine; grain on the sabbath; a withered hand; and now twelve names, first called to be with him.
screen: `TO BE WITH HIM, THEN TO BE SENT.` · `APOSTOLOS — ONE WHO IS SENT.` · `TWELVE, LIKE THE TRIBES.` · `A ROLL CALL THAT ENDS WITH JUDAS.`

segments.voice: Let names come, one at a time, like a roll call of twelve people who shaped you: a parent or grandparent, a teacher, a friend from a hard year, someone who hurt you and taught you something anyway, someone whose name you've forgotten but whose kindness you haven't. Don't rank them; if you get stuck, wait, and one more will come. If you pray, thank God for each name.
Apostle. From the Greek apostolos, one who is sent. In Mark, called first to be with him, then sent.
